scenes.title: What a prototype is for
scenes.narration: A prototype is not a small product. It is an instrument for retiring risk, and the only risk worth retiring is the kind you cannot undo. So the question this repository was built to answer is a narrow one: which decisions, taken wrongly, could not be walked back later — and were those the ones that got the engineering time.

scenes.title: The domain, as an engineering object
scenes.narration: Bed allocation is a constraint problem wearing clinical clothes. Five entities, a strict containment hierarchy from level to ward to bed, and a bed that is always in exactly one of four states. Six roles act on it. And three external systems it has to integrate with, none of which exist here. That last line is the whole engineering problem.

scenes.title: 02b-bed-board-capture
scenes.narration: This is the board those states drive. Not a dashboard — a state machine with a colour rendering. Every operation in the system is a legal transition between four states, and that is what makes the invariant checkable: a bed cannot leave one state without entering another, so it can never quietly go missing.

scenes.title: Both default moves fail
scenes.narration: The first option is to fake everything behind a beautiful interface. On camera that is indistinguishable from the genuine article, which means it demonstrates nothing. The second is to do the whole job for real — and that does not survive contact with what I actually had: no records endpoint, no identity tenant, no solver licence, no team, and nothing resembling production access.

scenes.title: The part that cannot be faked
scenes.narration: And this domain will not let you fake the part that matters. Put one man into an empty six-bed cubicle and the other five beds can now only take men. Get that wrong and the artifact is not unpolished, it is wrong — and any reviewer who knows the domain sees it in a second. So safety could not be a stub.

scenes.title: The seam is the deliverable
scenes.narration: Here is the rule I actually applied. Where a decision was reversible, I cut an interface first and put a mock behind it. Where it was not reversible, I built it. The seam is the deliverable; the adapter behind it is scheduling. And what that costs is real — only one side of the boundary is ever exercised, so the boundary is a promise, not a proof.

scenes.title: 05a-seam-diagram-capture
scenes.narration: Three seams, drawn the way the container wires them. One interface, two implementations: a mock that runs under the prototype profile, and a production adapter that exists, compiles, and refuses to do anything. The profile decides which one is loaded, once, at startup.

scenes.title: 05b-profile-fence-terminal
scenes.narration: That refusal is not theoretical. This is the same jar, started with the production profile. The health check answers, so the application is up — and every business endpoint comes back four-oh-three, because the only security configuration left authenticates everything and no login mechanism exists yet. Worth naming: the prototype profile is the default in configuration, so production is the profile you have to ask for. That is on the list of what is owed.

scenes.title: 05c-stub-contract-terminal
scenes.narration: And the stubs themselves are under test. Three production adapters, each asserted to throw the moment it is invoked. That is the part people skip — a placeholder nobody tests will eventually be called by accident, in a profile nobody checked.

scenes.title: 05d-persona-fence-capture
scenes.narration: One convenience was deliberately kept, and it is a security hole. Six personas, six seeded accounts, and a switch that changes role without a login. I built it because a reviewer has to walk five desks to see the argument, and five login flows would bury it. It is fenced behind the prototype profile, and the production configuration refuses that header outright.

scenes.title: A heuristic, not a constraint engine
scenes.narration: Second decision. The textbook answer for bed allocation is a constraint solver — Timefold. I know it, it fits, and I did not use it. It wants a licence, it wants a daemon solving continuously, and it answers a coordinator's question with a score I cannot decompose. So I wrote the heuristic, and I paid for it: this is not globally optimal, and at a large enough ward count it will be beaten.

scenes.title: 06a-explainable-score-capture
scenes.narration: Four hard rules filter the candidate set, then three weighted preferences rank what survives. Three beds come back for this patient — seventy, thirty and thirty — and under each score, the rules that produced it. That decomposition is the whole point of the trade: a coordinator can read why the first bed beat the other two, which is exactly what the solver could not have given me.

scenes.title: 06b-weights-are-config-capture
scenes.narration: And the weights are configuration, not code. Specialty alignment at forty points, cubicle consolidation at thirty, falls-risk proximity at fifteen — retunable while the hospital is running. When a dengue cluster changes what a good bed looks like, that should not need a software release.

scenes.title: 06c-solver-pinned-terminal
scenes.narration: The heuristic is pinned by tests, which is what makes it safe to throw away. Every rule has an assertion behind it — so the day Timefold goes in behind that interface, these are the tests it has to satisfy.

scenes.title: Safety is not overridable. Operations are.
scenes.narration: Third decision, and the one I would defend hardest. Constraints are not one list. Safety invariants are absolute; operational constraints are negotiable with a reason. The cost of that is deliberate — when a clinician is right and an invariant disagrees, the system offers no way through. I chose to make that a human conversation rather than a button.

scenes.title: 07a-absolute-tier-terminal
scenes.narration: Notice how the absolute tier gets proved. There is no disabled button to photograph, because a bed that violates a hard constraint never becomes a recommendation at all — it is eliminated from the candidate set. Absence cannot be screenshotted, so it is asserted: gender, telemetry, infection, negative pressure, each with a test that fails if that bed survives.

scenes.title: 07b-override-modal-capture
scenes.narration: The negotiable tier behaves differently. Taking anything other than the top-ranked bed forces a modal, and the modal will not close without a structured institutional code — not free text, because free text cannot be queried later. Confirming writes an immutable override record. Overridable, but never silent.

scenes.title: Direct mutation, with locking where it races
scenes.narration: Fourth decision, and I will lead with what it cost. I gave up the audit trail, the temporal queries and the replay that event sourcing hands you for free — in a domain where audit is a regulatory requirement. What I got back was a prototype one person can read: direct state mutation, version columns on the three entities two people actually race for, and conflicts surfaced as a 409.

scenes.title: 08b-conflict-409-terminal
scenes.narration: The concurrency claim is the one I cannot show you honestly in a browser. Two specialists claiming the same broadcast is a race, and a race staged in a single tab is a lie. So it is a test: two versions, one write, 409 Conflict, and a problem-detail body the client can actually act on.

scenes.title: Correctness had to be provable
scenes.narration: Fifth decision. Every operational metric is derivable twice — once from relational state for reporting, once from the structured audit log for alerting — and a test asserts that the two agree. The cost is two things to keep in step. And the honest limit on all of this: the backend has no coverage threshold at all, the frontend declares four, and nothing runs either of them automatically.

scenes.title: 09a-analytics-capture
scenes.narration: Pathway A. Twenty metrics across four epic sections, each with its benchmark and an evaluation against it, computed from relational state at request time. These are numbers the running system produced from the workflows in this film — not figures typed into a slide.

scenes.title: 09b-audit-log-terminal
scenes.narration: Pathway B is this. The same events, in the log, with the acting user carried in the mapped diagnostic context on every line. That format does not change between profiles — only the destination does. Today it is standard output. In production it is a SIEM, and nothing above the appender needs to know.

scenes.title: 09c-parity-terminal
scenes.narration: And parity is asserted, not eyeballed. The reconciliation test computes each metric down both pathways and fails when they disagree, which is the only thing that makes a second pathway worth having.

scenes.title: 09d-coverage-capture
scenes.narration: Measured, on the whole backend bundle: ninety-four percent of instructions, ninety-seven percent of lines — and sixty-nine percent of branches. That last number is the one worth saying out loud, because it is where the untested paths actually live. It is evidence the domain layer is exercised. It is not a quality gate.

scenes.title: 09e-gate-red-terminal
scenes.narration: And here is what that costs, right now. The frontend declares four coverage thresholds at ninety percent. Run them and one is red — branches at seventy-five. Nothing caught that, because nothing runs it. A gate no pipeline executes is not a gate; it is a comment with a number in it.

scenes.title: What is owed, and the seam it is owed against
scenes.narration: So here is what is owed. In-memory data that a restart erases. Polling that will not scale. A heuristic that is not optimal. Personas that are not authentication. A prototype profile that is the configuration default. And a coverage threshold that is failing right now because nothing runs it. Each one has its seam already cut, and that is the only reason I can list them this calmly. On method: AI wrote a great deal of this code. Which trade-off to take, which approach was better, and what the final code looks like — those were mine.
